analysis.one_liner: Caps soft-money contributions to national political parties at $10,000 per person per year, restricts nonprofit 'issue' fundraising by candidates and parties, broadens which campaign ads count as regulated independent expenditures, and requires large fundraising committees to file monthly reports online.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee in the 105th Congress, with no vote ever taken in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was the Democratic leadership's response to the 1996 campaign finance scandals. It would have capped unlimited 'soft money' donations to national party committees at $10,000 per person per year, redefined which pre-election issue ads count as regulated campaign expenditures, barred candidates and parties from soliciting money for tax-exempt 501(c) nonprofit groups, and required candidates raising over $50,000 to file monthly campaign-finance reports online. It was introduced by House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt (D-MO) with 102 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Oversight Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want big-money influence out of elections benefit from the soft-money cap and disclosure requirements. The $10,000 cap on soft money would shrink the six- and seven-figure checks from corporations, unions, and wealthy donors that funded party 'issue advocacy' after the 1996 election. The 501(c) solicitation ban targets the loophole where candidates raised tax-deductible dollars for 'educational' nonprofits like the Democratic National Committee-affiliated groups exposed in the 1996 fundraising scandal. Monthly online filing would have made campaign money visible to voters in near real time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters seeking transparency in party fundraising

how_it_helps.text: Caps individual soft-money payments to national party committees at $10,000 per year, versus unlimited before. [S3] SEC. 2
Bars candidates, officeholders, and party committees from soliciting or donating to 501(c) tax-exempt nonprofits, closing a route used for tax-deductible 'issue' money. [S3] SEC. 4
Deems communications naming a candidate within 90 days of an election (over $10,000 spent) to be independent expenditures subject to federal limits, closing the issue-advocacy loophole. [S3] SEC. 3
Requires candidates raising $50,000+ to file monthly reports and post them online, making contributions visible to voters well before election day. [S3] SEC. 5

analysis.who_pays: Large donors and political parties bear the cost: corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals would lose the ability to give unlimited soft money, parties would lose those funds, and candidates would face higher compliance burdens from monthly electronic filing. Tax-exempt nonprofits tied to candidates lose a fundraising channel.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big donors, party committees, and nonprofits

drawbacks.text: The soft-money cap would push large donations toward hard-money limits and independent groups, potentially accelerating the shift to outside spending rather than reducing overall money in politics.
Monthly electronic filing imposes real compliance costs on campaigns without obviously improving enforcement, since FEC enforcement was already weak.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, incremental reform bill — smaller in scope than the McCain-Feingold-style full soft-money ban proposals, and narrower than the bipartisan Shays-Meehan / Meehan-Feingold bills moving in the House at the time. It tackles real 1996 loopholes (soft money, 501(c) issue ads, nonprofit laundering) but does not change hard-money limits or create public financing, so its overall effect on money in politics would have been partial.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the House Oversight Committee on introduction day and never reported out, dying when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Introduced October 30, 1997, by House Minority Leader Gephardt and 102 other House Democrats. [S1]
Referred to the House Committee on House Oversight (then chaired by Rep. Thomas Bliley, R-VA) the same day; no further action was ever recorded. [S5]
The 105th Congress ended January 3, 1999, with the bill still in committee. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Big donors and party committees are better off: unlimited soft money and issue-advocacy spending continued through the 1998 and 2000 elections until McCain-Feingold passed in 2002.

for.name: Richard A. Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as the Democratic leadership's reform proposal following the 1996 fundraising controversies.

against.name: House Committee on House Oversight
against.what_they_did: Took no action; the bill was never reported, never scheduled for markup or floor vote, and died in committee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 102 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never advanced it.

industries.note: Would lose unlimited soft-money revenue under the $10,000 cap and lose a nonprofit fundraising channel. Parties' institutional interest in unregulated money ran against voters' interest in disclosure and contribution limits.

Would lose the ability to channel unlimited soft money and tax-deductible 'issue' donations to influence elections. Their interest in preserving access runs against voters' interest in equal political voice.
Would lose the ability to receive candidate- or party-solicited funds. These groups had become a vehicle for unregulated 'issue' money after 1996.
